title.label: Feels More Focused on Revenue Than User Experience

content.label:
This was recommended by a ADHD youtuber, so I tried the Endel app after his recommendation. Unfortunately, my experience was the opposite of what I expected.
The subscription model was the first red flag. Even though I downloaded it through the App Store, I had to enter my credit card directly instead of subscribing through Apple. If someone forgets to cancel the 7-day trial, they’re charged $119 for a year. I only used the app for a few minutes before deciding it wasn’t for me and canceled right away, but the whole setup felt intentionally designed to make it easier for people to end up paying.

Before I even had a chance to understand what the app actually did, it was asking me to invite three friends. That immediately gave me the impression that getting new users is a higher priority than letting people experience the product first (which also hints that the developers are not very confident in the product itself, because if the product was great, people would recommend it to friends and family without prompting)

The app is also marketed for people with ADHD, but I found the interface overwhelming rather than helpful. There are lots of menus and options to click through without much guidance. I tapped “Anxiety Relief,” expecting some explanation or immediate experience, but it simply asked me to set a timer. Then I was looking at a black screen with a few dots and, at least in my case, no sound at all. I was left wondering whether I had missed something. Instead of feeling supported, I felt confused.

Overall, the app felt like a basic library of ambient sounds with very little explanation of what makes it worth $119 a year. The black screen with gray and white elements also felt claustrophobic to me rather than calming. I kept wondering what I was paying for that I couldn’t get elsewhere.

What I found most ironic is that this app was recommended in a video about doing less and avoiding unnecessary additions to your life. To me, this app is exactly that—another subscription, another account, another thing to manage, without offering enough value to justify it.

My issue is not just that the app is overpriced. The issue is the billing flow. I downloaded Endel believing I was starting a free trial. I did not knowingly agree to a paid annual subscription or knowingly authorize a $119.99 charge. After the charge appeared, I immediately checked my Apple Subscriptions to cancel or manage it, but there was no active or past Endel subscription listed there.

That matters. Most iPhone users reasonably assume that if they download an app from the App Store and authorize payment through an Apple-looking flow, the subscription will appear under Apple Subscriptions. In my case, it did not. That means I could not cancel, verify, or manage the charge through the standard Apple subscription process.

This is especially concerning because Endel markets itself toward people with ADHD and focus difficulties. A confusing trial/payment/cancellation flow is bad for any user, but it is especially harmful when the app is being advertised to people who may already struggle with memory, task-switching, and subscription management.

The ads I saw also emphasized special “8D” audio/music content. What I found in the app did not match what was advertised. Other reviews describe similar issues: people expected the advertised 8D tracks or trial experience and instead ended up confused, disappointed, or charged.

If you already got charged and cannot find Endel under Apple Subscriptions, this is the dispute language I recommend giving your bank or card issuer:

“I am disputing a $119.99 charge from Endel. I did not knowingly authorize a paid annual subscription and did not provide informed consent to be charged this amount. I initially downloaded the Endel app under what was presented as a free trial. After seeing the charge, I immediately attempted to locate and cancel any associated subscription. However, there is no active or past Endel subscription listed under my Apple Subscriptions. Because the subscription does not appear in Apple’s subscription management system, I was unable to cancel, verify, or manage it through the normal Apple subscription process. For these reasons, I believe this charge resulted from a deceptive or unclear billing flow, and I request a full refund.”

This app should not be allowed to advertise a simple free-trial experience while using a payment and cancellation structure that many users cannot reasonably understand or manage. Be extremely careful before entering any trial or payment flow.
